question: The Waldstatte Alliance concluded in 1291 between Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden was sealed by which document?

options.C: the Federal Treaty of 1815
options.D: the Federal Constitution of 1848

source_quote: In 1291, the three cantons of Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden concluded the regional Waldstätte Alliance, which was sealed by the Federal Charter of 1291.
notes: Distractors C and D are real Swiss foundational documents, which is what makes the 1291 charter easy to confuse. Source URL is bar.admin.ch, a federal archive substitution for the blocked eda.admin.ch history page.

question: When the Helvetian Republic was proclaimed in 1798 under French occupation, which institution — described as a predecessor of today's Swiss Federal Archives — was established at the same time?

options.C: the Federal Mint
options.D: the Federal Chancellery

source_quote: The Central Archives, a predecessor of the current Swiss Federal Archives, were also established during this time.
notes: Distractors are all real Swiss federal institutions that simply do not date from 1798.

question: Switzerland's neutrality is recognised worldwide. What is Switzerland therefore often asked to do?

options.A: contribute troops to United Nations peacekeeping forces
options.B: host the headquarters of a NATO body
options.C: mediate in conflicts or exercise protective power mandates
options.D: take part in the collective defence commitments of an alliance

source_quote: Switzerland's neutrality is recognised worldwide, which is why it is often asked to mediate in conflicts or exercise protective power mandates.
notes: Mediation and protective power mandates are classic Swiss neutrality roles; the options that assume alliance or UN membership are the standard EU/NATO import error.

question: Switzerland is not a member of NATO. Within which two frameworks does it nevertheless cooperate with NATO?

options.A: the Partnership for Peace and the Western European Union
options.B: the European Union's Common Security and Defence Policy and the Western European Union
options.C: the Organisation for Security and Co-operation in Europe and the Council of Europe
options.D: the Partnership for Peace and the Euro-Atlantic Partnership Council

source_quote: Switzerland is not a member of NATO, but cooperates with it within the framework of the Partnership for Peace and the Euro-Atlantic Partnership Council.
notes: Shared page with S041; NATO non-membership plus PfP/EAPC cooperation is a specifically Swiss arrangement.

question: Under which constitutional instrument did the Swiss Federal Supreme Court become a permanent court?

options.A: the 1874 Constitution, which came into force in 1875
options.C: the total revision approved by voters in 1999
options.D: the partial revision of 1866

source_quote: It was only with the 1874 Constitution, which came into force in 1875, that the Swiss Federal Supreme Court became a permanent court
notes: Caveat: the 1848 federal state already had a supreme court, but it had no fixed seat and only convened as and when required.

question: Why was the seat of the Swiss Federal Supreme Court assigned to Lausanne rather than to Zurich, Bern or Lucerne?

options.A: Because Lausanne was the largest city in French-speaking Switzerland.
options.B: As a concession to the French-speaking liberals.
options.C: Because the cantonal government of Vaud paid for the building.
options.D: Because the first president of the court came from Lausanne.

source_quote: As a concession to the French-speaking liberals, the seat of the Swiss Federal Supreme Court was assigned to Lausanne.
notes: A strong trap: the court does have a second site in Lucerne, but Lucerne was never the seat, and neither was Zurich or the federal city Bern.

question: In which year did the Federal Supreme Court move into the Neoclassical building in the Mon-Repos park that still houses it today?
source_quote: Due to the outbreak of the First World War, the new courthouse could not be built until 1922. The striking Neoclassical building in the Mon-Repos park still shapes our image of the Swiss Federal Supreme Court today.
notes: 1887 is the year the court moved into the purpose-built structure on the Esplanade de Montbenon — a deliberate near-miss distractor.

question: The Swiss Federal Supreme Court ruled that women from which canton must be granted the right to vote at the cantonal assembly?

options.C: Appenzell Innerrhoden
options.D: Obwalden

source_quote: The Swiss Federal Supreme Court rules that women from the canton of Appenzell Innerrhoden be granted the right to vote at the cantonal assembly. On 28 April 1991, women in Appenzell Innerrhoden were also able to vote in cantonal elections for the first time. BGE 116 Ia 359
notes: Appenzell Innerrhoden is one of the six half-cantons and the last to hold out. The brochure does not date the ruling itself, only the cantonal election of 28 April 1991, so no year is asserted here. Appenzell Innerrhoden is deliberately not used in the S040 questions to avoid duplicate facts.

question: On what date did Switzerland's all-male electorate grant the vote to the nation's female citizens?

options.C: 14 June 1971
options.D: 28 April 1991

source_quote: On 7 February 1971, Switzerland's all-male electorate granted the vote to the nation's female citizens.
notes: 1 February 1959 is the first (rejected) federal suffrage vote and 28 April 1991 the Appenzell Innerrhoden cantonal election — both genuine dates used as distractors.

question: Switzerland's first federal vote on women's suffrage failed by a large margin. What share of those who cast their ballots voted against it?
source_quote: The first vote at federal level in 1959 failed by a large margin, with 67% of those who cast their ballots against.
notes: 33% is the share of men still voting no in 1971; 55% recurs in S041/S049 as the 2002 UN and 2005 Bilaterals II yes shares.

question: The petition presented in Bern in 1929 by the Swiss Association for Women's Suffrage carried how many signatures?

options.C: 249,200 in total — 170,400 from women and 78,800 from men
options.D: 249,200 in total — 78,800 from women and 170,400 from men

source_quote: In 1929, the Swiss Association for Women's Suffrage presented a petition in Bern signed by 170,400 women and 78,800 men. Parliament backed the petition, but the Federal Council chose not to pursue it.
notes: Note the men-to-women inversion distractor D. Parliament supported the petition but the Federal Council declined to pursue it.

question: In which year did Swiss voters reject membership of the European Economic Area (EEA)?
source_quote: Swiss voters rejected membership of the EEA in 1992.
notes: 1986 is the rejected UN initiative year (S049); 2000 is the Bilaterals I year. Switzerland is in EFTA and Schengen but not in the EEA or the EU.

question: The Schengen and Dublin agreements were part of which series of Swiss bilateral agreements with the EU, and in which year was that series approved by voters?

options.C: the second series, approved in 2002
options.D: the first series, approved in 2005

source_quote: There are 9 agreements, including the Schengen-Dublin agreement, which was approved by 55 % of voters in 2005.
notes: The first series (2000) comprised 7 mainly economic agreements; the second series (2005) comprises 9 and was approved by 55 %. Note the source's spacing in '55 %'.

question: The first Geneva Convention, adopted in August 1864, introduced a unified emblem for military medical services. What did that emblem look like?

options.A: a white cross on a red background
options.B: a red cross on a white background
options.C: a red crescent on a white background
options.D: a red cross on a black background

source_quote: And in August 1864 it persuaded governments to adopt the first Geneva Convention. This treaty obliged armies to care for wounded soldiers, whatever side they were on, and introduced a unified emblem for the medical services: a red cross on a white background.
notes: Distractor A is the actual Swiss flag; the emblem is its colour inverse. The source states only the colours, not the inversion — the inverse relationship must be inferred. The red crescent is the real alternative emblem used by the Red Crescent societies.

question: In which years was the International Committee of the Red Cross awarded the Nobel Peace Prize?

options.D: 1917, 1944 and again in 1963, the last together with the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies

source_quote: The ICRC was then awarded the Nobel Prize in 1917 and 1944, as a tribute to its humanitarian activities during the two World Wars, and again in 1963, together with the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies.
notes: The Nobel quote comes from the second ICRC page recorded in the same raw_pages file. Distractor A mixes in Henry Dunant's 1901 prize, which went to him personally, not to the ICRC.

question: ETH Zurich was established in 1855. Under which name was it founded?

options.C: Federal Polytechnic School
options.D: Swiss Federal School of Engineering

source_quote: Established in 1855 as the Federal Polytechnic School, ETH Zurich has, from the outset, been a national centre for education with international appeal, attracting talent from all over the world.
notes: Distractor A is the name it has held since 1911. S043 has only four verified facts, so this file supplies just one question.

question: On what date did the people and the cantons approve the 1999 total revision of the Federal Constitution?

options.D: 1 January 2000

source_quote: This total revision was approved by the People and the cantons on 18 April 1999 by majorities of 59.2% and 14 out of 26 cantons respectively.
notes: It came into force on 1 January 2000 (distractor D). The quote is from the parlament.ch Federal Constitution page recorded verbatim inside the S048 raw_pages file; ch-info.swiss is the header URL of that file. 14 of 26 cantons is a majority but not an overwhelming one.

question: Before the 1999 total revision of the Federal Constitution, where were Swiss fundamental rights to be found in law?

options.A: In a single article of the Federal Constitution of 1848
options.B: In decisions of the Federal Supreme Court and in legal commentaries
options.C: In the Federal Treaty of 1815
options.D: In the constitutions of the cantons only

source_quote: among other new provisions contained articles on fundamental rights that had previously only been set out in decisions of the Federal Supreme Court and legal commentaries
notes: Unwritten constitutional law codified in 1999 — a specifically Swiss feature with no German or Austrian equivalent in this form. Quote again from the parlament.ch page embedded in the S048 file.

question: On what date did Swiss voters approve joining the United Nations?

options.C: 3 March 2002
options.D: 16 March 1986

source_quote: When, on March 3, 2002, the Swiss were again called upon to vote on joining the world body, the decision turned out to be quite close.
notes: Verified: referendum 3 March 2002; the UN General Assembly accepted Switzerland as the 190th member state on 10 September 2002 (distractor B). Distractor A, 10 March 2002, is the disproved date recorded in the verification log. 16 March 1986 was an earlier rejected initiative. swissinfo.ch is the Swiss Broadcasting Corporation, not a federal page.

question: Which international treaty first set out in writing the rights and duties of neutral states?

options.C: The United Nations Charter of 1945
options.D: The Hague Conventions of 1907

source_quote: In 1907, the Hague Conventions set out in writing the rights and duties of neutral states for the first time.
notes: Replaces an earlier K120 (1815 / Congress of Vienna), which the drafting agent and the reviewer both flagged as well-known general knowledge rather than Swiss-specific knowledge. This item anchors Swiss neutrality in international law - which is the verified position, since neutrality was never codified in a Swiss statute. Distractors A and D are both real treaties that a model may reach for.

question: According to the Federal Chancellery, what did the Federal Treaty of 1815 do to the various federal alliances that had grown up in Switzerland over the centuries?

options.A: It dissolved them and replaced them with a Helvetian Republic administered from Paris.
options.B: It brought them together into a single confederation of states.
options.C: It turned them into 22 sovereign cantons with full legislative independence.
options.D: It placed them under the joint administration of the Allied powers.

source_quote: The Federal Treaty of 1815 brought together the various federal alliances into a single confederation of states.
notes: Distractor A imports the 1798 Helvetian Republic and is the standard European-generalities error; C assumes a unitary cantonal state that did not exist; D is the 'Switzerland was a puppet' reflex. The 1815 instrument consolidated alliances, it did not dissolve them.

question: Following the defeat of Napoleon, what did the great European powers do to Switzerland's borders in 1815?

options.A: They extended them southward to include the whole of the canton of Ticino.
options.B: They fixed them at the Rhine and the Alps, and added the principality of Vaduz.
options.C: They granted Switzerland a permanent corridor to the Adriatic through the Gotthard.
options.D: They set Switzerland's borders as they are today.

source_quote: With the defeat of Napoleon, the great European powers recognised Swiss neutrality and set Switzerland's borders as they are today.
notes: B is the Liechtenstein trap and conflates the 1815 settlement with Liechtenstein's 1806 entry into the French sphere; A and C are the 'Alpine fortress with an outlet' fantasy that models reach for. Borders AND neutrality were settled together in 1815, which is the point of the item.

question: How did the architects of the Swiss constitution of 1848 understand Swiss neutrality?

options.A: As a tool for maintaining the country's independence.
options.B: As a legal obligation imposed from abroad by the Congress of Vienna.
options.C: As a temporary arrangement to be renounced once the territory was secure.
options.D: As an inherited privilege of the Swiss Confederation's three founding cantons.

source_quote: For the architects of the Swiss constitution of 1848, neutrality was a tool for maintaining the country's independence.
notes: B and C are the two textbook misreadings - that neutrality was externally imposed, or that it was a wartime expedient. The quote is from the swissinfo.ch neutrality page recorded verbatim inside the S050 file, so it is the broadcaster's reading of 1848, not settled constitutional scholarship. A neutral state operates a legal status; it is not the recipient of a favour.

question: Under the 1907 Hague Conventions, what did neutral states owe in exchange for the inviolability of their territory?

options.A: The right to supply arms and troops to whichever belligerent paid for them.
options.B: An obligation to grant belligerents the use of their airspace and ports.
options.C: A duty to stay out of wars, to treat all belligerents equally, and not to supply them with arms or troops.
options.D: A duty to enforce the peace settlement on both sides of the conflict.

source_quote: In exchange for the inviolability of their territory, such countries were, among other things, bound to stay out of wars, to treat all belligerents equally and not to supply them with arms or troops.
notes: A and B treat neutrality as commerce and access, which is exactly the misunderstanding: neutrality is a reciprocity, not a trade. K120 asks which treaty first codified these rights; this item asks what the bargain was, so the two do not overlap. Quote comes from the swissinfo.ch page recorded in the S050 file.

question: Why did the Swiss government rule out membership when the United Nations was founded in 1945?

options.A: It saw the organisation as dominated by the former Axis powers.
options.B: It saw the organisation as incompatible with neutrality.
options.C: It saw the organisation as incompatible with Switzerland's membership of the European Free Trade Association.
options.D: It saw the organisation as incompatible with Switzerland's federal structure.

source_quote: When the UN was founded in 1945, the Swiss government ruled out membership. It saw the organisation as incompatible with neutrality.
notes: C and D are invented but sound like constitutional reasoning, which is what makes them dangerous. A is the generic bloc-politics default. swissinfo.ch is the Swiss Broadcasting Corporation, not a federal page, so the item is framed as what the source states; no date for a later policy reversal is asserted.

question: According to swissinfo.ch, from what date has Switzerland held observer status in the main organs of the United Nations?
source_quote: Switzerland has enjoyed observer status in the main organs of the UN since 1948.
notes: 1945 (UN founding) and 2002 (accession) are the two dates a model reaches for by default; 1992 is the EEA rejection year borrowed from S041. Observer status from 1948 sits in the gap between them and is the least guessable of the four.

question: When the UN General Assembly accepted Switzerland as its 190th member state in 2002, which state did that leave as the only one outside the United Nations?

options.C: the Sovereign Order of Malta
options.D: Monaco

source_quote: On September 10, 2002, the UN General Assembly in New York accepted Switzerland as the 190th member state. This left the Vatican as the only state outside the United Nations.
notes: Liechtenstein is the classic wrong answer - a microstate wedged between Switzerland and Austria that is also outside the UN. C and D are real non-member states but were never the last one out. Note the two-step reasoning: accession as the 190th member is what produced the claim about the Vatican.

question: On what date did Swiss voters first reject a national initiative on joining the United Nations, before the successful 2002 vote?

options.C: 3 March 1992
options.D: 16 March 1986

source_quote: At the ballot box on March 16, 1986 they clearly rejected the initiative.
notes: C borrows the day-and-month pattern of the successful 2002 vote and pairs it with the wrong year (1992 is the EEA rejection); A shifts the year by a decade; B is the rejected 1959 federal women's suffrage vote from S040, a cross-domain confusion a non-expert would make confidently.

question: Which previous Federal Constitution did the total revision approved in 1999 replace?

options.C: the Federal Constitution of 29 May 1874
options.D: the Federal Treaty of 1815

source_quote: It replaced the previous Federal Constitution of 29 May 1874
notes: A is the near-universal wrong answer because 1848 is the constitution that established the federal state, but that text had already been overtaken by the 1874 total revision. B is a partial revision, not a superseded constitution. The quote is from the parlament.ch Federal Constitution page recorded verbatim inside the S048 file.

question: On what date did the third Federal Constitution, approved by voters in 1999, come into force?

options.C: 1 January 1999
options.D: 1 January 2000

source_quote: It came into force on 1 January 2000.
notes: The approval date (18 April 1999) is distractor B and is already used as the answer in K117 - the gap between approval and entry into force is the whole trap. D pairs the 1874 constitution with the wrong effective year.

question: Which federal democratic instrument was introduced by the first total revision of the Federal Constitution, which came into force in 1874?

options.C: the election of the Federal Council by popular vote
options.D: the cantonal right to legislate on foreign affairs

source_quote: The first total revision came into force in 1874. It introduced wider powers for the federal government and gave more democratic rights to the electorate. This total revision also introduced the referendum at federal level.
notes: Distractor A is the single most-swapped fact in Swiss direct democracy: the popular initiative came in 1891, seventeen years after the referendum. C and D are inventions that sound federal. ch-info.swiss gives both years in the same passage.

question: By what majorities did the people and the cantons approve the 1999 total revision of the Federal Constitution?

options.A: 59.2% of the people and 20 out of 26 cantons
options.B: 50.5% of the people and 13 out of 26 cantons
options.C: 59.2% of the people and 14 out of 26 cantons
options.D: 59.2% of the people and 14 out of 22 cantons

source_quote: This total revision was approved by the People and the cantons on 18 April 1999 by majorities of 59.2% and 14 out of 26 cantons respectively.
notes: 14 of 26 cantons is a cantonal majority but a much thinner one than the 59.2% popular majority, and models overstate it as a landslide. Distractors A and D each inflate the cantonal or dilute the denominator. Quote is from the parlament.ch page embedded in the S048 file; K117 already used this passage for the date.

question: Henry Dunant, one of the five members who met in Geneva in February 1863, had published a book the year before. What was it called?

options.C: A Memory of Solferino
options.D: The Battle of Solferino

source_quote: Among its five members was a local man named Henry Dunant who, the year before, had published a book (A Souvenir of Solferino) calling for improved care for wounded soldiers in wartime.
notes: B is the original French title and C a plausible anglicisation, so both are confidently reachable; D is the battle itself rather than the account of it. The source gives the English form. Note the ICRC page deliberately does not describe the emblem as an inverse of the Swiss flag, so that claim is not asserted here either.

question: Where and when was the first national Red Cross society established?

options.A: in the German State of Württemberg in November 1863
options.B: in the German State of Württemberg in November 1864
options.C: in the Kingdom of Saxony in November 1863
options.D: in the Austrian Empire in November 1863

source_quote: Over the following 50 years, the ICRC expanded its work while national societies were established (the first in the German State of Württemberg in November 1863) and the Geneva Convention was adapted to include warfare at sea.
notes: The date is the trap: the ICRC's own first meeting (February 1863) and the first Geneva Convention (August 1864) bracket the true November 1863. Württemberg, Saxony and the Austrian Empire are all plausible German-speaking states of the period; only Württemberg is named by the source.

question: The fourth Geneva Convention, agreed in 1949 at the ICRC's initiative, covered which category of person?

options.A: wounded and sick on the battlefield
options.C: victims of war at sea
options.D: civilians living under enemy control

source_quote: In 1949, at the ICRC's initiative, states agreed on the revision of the existing three Geneva Conventions (covering wounded and sick on the battlefield, victims of war at sea, prisoners of war) and the addition of a fourth: to protect civilians living under enemy control.
notes: Every distractor is the subject of one of the three existing conventions revised at the same moment, which is the standard conflation - the 1949 package was revision plus addition, not four new treaties. The ICRC's initiative, not a state's, is what makes this a specifically Swiss-driven step.

question: Which body did the Red Cross national societies found in 1919 as the future coordinating and support body of the Movement?

options.A: the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies
options.B: the League of Nations' humanitarian commission
options.C: the League of Red Cross Societies
options.D: the International Committee of the Red Cross

source_quote: In 1919, they founded the League of Red Cross Societies, intended as the future coordinating and support body for the Movement.
notes: The International Federation also dates from 1919, so A matches on the year and is the strongest trap in this item; the ICRC (D) appears in the same page and never founded it. This is the most confused corner of the Movement's institutional history and is a Swiss-specific fact rather than a European generality.

question: How many agreements made up the first series of Swiss bilateral agreements with the EU, approved by voters in 2000?
source_quote: The first series of bilateral agreements was accepted by 67% of Swiss voters in 2000. The 7 agreements mainly cover economic matters.
notes: 9 is the count for the second series of 2005, which contains Schengen-Dublin - the two series are routinely swapped, and K113 already used the second series. Switzerland's EU relations run on over 100 bilateral agreements, which invites a larger number than either series.

question: Which states, together with the EU countries, form the European Economic Area?

options.C: All EFTA countries plus Switzerland and Liechtenstein
options.D: The EFTA countries together with the United Kingdom

source_quote: Together with the EU countries, the EFTA countries – excluding Switzerland – form the European Economic Area (EEA).
notes: Switzerland is an EFTA member and a Schengen member but sits outside the EEA as a direct consequence of the 1992 rejection, and models fold it in because of the EFTA membership. C double-counts Switzerland; D assumes the UK found a home in EFTA after leaving the EU. Source: Federal Chancellery brief guide 2024.

question: According to the Federal Chancellery's brief guide, where is the United Nations headquartered?

options.A: Main headquarters in Geneva, with European offices in New York and Vienna
options.B: Main headquarters in New York, with European headquarters in Geneva and Vienna
options.C: Main headquarters in New York, with European headquarters in Geneva only
options.D: Main headquarters in Vienna, with European offices in Geneva and New York

source_quote: Main headquarters in New York, European headquarters in Geneva and Vienna
notes: A is the single most common UN error, produced by Geneva's weight as a diplomatic and humanitarian hub. C drops Vienna, which is easy to do because Vienna is usually attached to the IAEA rather than to the UN. The same source line also gives 194 member states and a 1945 founding, neither of which is asked here.

question: The Council of Europe was founded in 1949. In which year did Switzerland join it?
source_quote: Council of Europe … Founded in 1949, Switzerland a member since 1963
notes: C and D are the confident wrong answers, borrowed from the EEA rejection and the UN accession. A is a plausible mid-century guess. The Council of Europe is a Strasbourg-based treaty organisation and is not the EU's Council - the conflation that produces most of the noise here.

question: According to the Federal Chancellery's brief guide 2024, which four states are the members of the European Free Trade Association?

options.C: Switzerland, Liechtenstein, Norway and the United Kingdom
options.D: Switzerland, Austria, Iceland and Norway

source_quote: The European Free Trade Association promotes free trade between its members Switzerland, Liechtenstein, Iceland and Norway.
notes: Finland (B) is the trap - EFTA is Nordic-Baltic but not the Nordic Council, and a model that reasons 'Nordic countries' will reach for it. C assumes the UK found a home in EFTA after leaving the EU; D substitutes Austria on geographic proximity. Every member listed here is also a micro or small state, which the distractors break.

question: In the sequence of Swiss constitutional development described by the Federal Chancellery, what stage came immediately before the federal state?

options.B: a permanent Federal Diet representing 22 cantons
options.C: a confederation of states
options.D: an Austrian crown land under Habsburg administration

source_quote: Switzerland developed over the centuries from a collection of different alliances to a confederation of states and finally to the federal state we know today.
notes: The three-stage sequence alliances then confederation of states then federal state is the point; A is the real 1798 interlude but not the immediate predecessor in this chain, and C and D are generic European-state inventions with no Swiss referent.

question: Which former special court was integrated into the Swiss Federal Supreme Court in 2007?

options.C: the Federal Banking Commission
options.D: the Federal Insurance Court (EVG)

source_quote: In 2007, the former Swiss Federal Insurance Court (EVG) was integrated into the Swiss Federal Supreme Court.
notes: A and B are still separate federal bodies, which is what makes them attractive; both also sound like plausible absorptions because they are real Swiss courts. The insurance appeals court is the one that was taken in, and its name is unlikely to be recalled unprompted. The same sentence attributes the strengthening of the Court's independence to the 1999 Constitution.

question: At the beginning of its existence, the nine federal judges working in the Casino de Derrière-Bourg were supported by how many court clerks?

options.C: two
options.D: twenty

source_quote: At the beginning of its existence, a total of nine federal judges worked in a room of the former casino, the 'Casino de Derrière-Bourg'. These regular judges were prohibited from engaging in any other activity. They were supported by two court clerks.
notes: D is the modern number of federal judges and about 175 is the present-day clerk count, so the confusable figures are both in the source; nine is the judge count and B is the copy-across trap. The 1863 two-clerk detail is the kind of concrete number a model will never have.

question: Why did the surrounding German-speaking regions come to refer to all Swiss confederates by the name of a single canton?

options.A: Because Schwyz was the largest of the three founding cantons.
options.B: Because Uri was the seat of the Federal Diet and issued the earliest federal charters.
options.C: Because the Schwyzers were famous for their role in the Waldstätte Alliance and for their mercenary troops.
options.D: Because Unterwalden supplied the largest contingent to the Swiss armies serving abroad.

source_quote: The Schwyzer, or Switzers, soon became well known far and wide thanks to the significant role they played in the Waldstätte Alliance and the importance of their troops as mercenaries. As a result, the surrounding German-speaking regions started to refer to all confederates as “Schwyzer”.
notes: A is the natural-sounding wrong answer: Schwyz is the canton named, but the source credits role and mercenaries, not size, and the etymology runs from “Schwyzer” to “Schweizer”. C and D attach the distinction to the other two founding cantons. K101 already used the 1291 alliance from this page, so this is a different fact from the same source.

question: Swiss mercenary service was outlawed in connection with which event?

options.B: the proclamation of the Helvetian Republic in 1798
options.C: the founding of the Federal State
options.D: the adoption of the first Geneva Convention in 1864

source_quote: The mercenaries had their heyday between the 15th and 18th century before being outlawed with the founding of the Federal State.
notes: A and B are the two big Swiss constitutional turning points and both are wrong here; D is a Swiss-adjacent date that appears on a different page entirely. The same sentence dates the heyday to the 15th to 18th century, so the two halves of the fact travel together.

question: At the 1971 federal vote on women's suffrage, roughly what share of men still voted no?

options.C: one half
options.D: one third

source_quote: Women’s dogged persistence, social liberalisation and pressure from abroad helped turn the tide, and in 1971 most men voted yes, with one third still in the 'no' camp.
notes: Deliberately paired with K110, which uses 33% as the distractor for the 1959 vote against; a model that swaps them has learned nothing about the sequence. The distinctive detail is that Switzerland passed only after most of Europe had already done so.

question: What made Switzerland an outlier when its first federal women's suffrage vote was held in 1959?

options.A: Women already had the vote in all six of the cantons that had piloted women's suffrage.
options.B: Women had not yet been given the vote anywhere in continental Europe.
options.C: Women already had the vote in all 26 of the Swiss cantons.
options.D: Women already had the vote across almost all of Europe.

source_quote: The first vote at federal level in 1959 failed by a large margin, with 67% of those who cast their ballots against. By that time, women had been given the vote across almost all of Europe.
notes: B and D are contradicted by the same page: the 1971 federal vote is what extended the right beyond the cantons, and Appenzell Innerrhoden lagged until 1991 (see S039). The real fact is the counterintuitive one - Switzerland trailed most of Europe on a question Europe had largely settled.

question: In which year was ETH Zurich given its present name, the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology?
source_quote: ETH Zurich was given its present name, Swiss Federal Institute of Technology (Eidgenössische Technische Hochschule), in 1911.
notes: 1855 is the founding year and already the answer context in K116; 1891 is the year the Swiss popular initiative was introduced (S048); 1961 is the Hönggerberg item, K300. The page gives only four verified facts, so this source supplies just two items.

question: In which year did ETH Zurich begin the first stage of constructing its second site, on the Hönggerberg?
source_quote: The university grew steadily and in 1961 it embarked on the first stage of constructing its second site on the Hönggerberg, on the outskirts of Zurich.
notes: B and C are the two other dates the same page supplies, and D is a plausible end-of-the-decades guess. The Hönggerberg detail matters because ETH is commonly assumed to have been a single downtown campus from 1855, which is the Swiss-education version of the European-generalities default.
